plan.contextChunk: This figure contains two panels, (a) and (b), illustrating the disk method for computing the volume of a solid of revolution. Panel (a): the 2D xy-plane showing region R bounded above by the curve y = f(x), below by the x-axis, and between x = a and x = b; a rotation arrow at x = b indicates revolution about the x-axis. Panel (b): a 3D perspective of the resulting solid; at a generic position x along the axis, a circular disk cross-section is highlighted in blue with radius f(x) labeled, showing that each cross-section perpendicular to the x-axis is a disk of area pi[f(x)]^2. The figure derives the disk method formula V = integral from a to b of pi[f(x)]^2 dx by identifying the cross-sectional area at each x and integrating along the axis of revolution.

interactions.label: Function and interval
interactions.teaches: The whole solid is determined by the curve y=f(x) on the interval [a,b]; at every x the disk radius is f(x), so changing the formula or the bounds changes both the shaded region and the resulting solid

interactions.label: Cross-section x
interactions.teaches: Sweeping along the interval shows that each perpendicular slice is a disk whose radius is f(x) and whose area is pi[f(x)]^2

interactions.label: View

demo_steps.title: Start with the generating region
demo_steps.narration: The shaded region R lies under y=f(x), above the x-axis, from a to b. This is the region that will be revolved around the x-axis.

demo_steps.title: Show the revolved solid
demo_steps.narration: After rotation about the x-axis, the same graph becomes the outer profile of the solid. The radius of the solid at any position x is exactly f(x).

demo_steps.title: Sweep a disk cross-section
demo_steps.narration: Move the highlighted disk along the x-axis. Its radius and area update as f(x) and pi[f(x)]^2, which is the quantity integrated in the disk method.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Use default function f(x)=sqrt(x), a=0.25, b=4. World-space convention: +X is screen-right along the axis of revolution, +Y is screen-up, +Z is depth around the x-axis. Panel (a) is a flat XY drawing in the z=0 plane: x-axis from X=-0.5 to X=4.8 at Y=0; y-axis at X=-0.15 from Y=-0.9 to Y=2.45; region spans X=0.25 to X=4 and Y=0 to sqrt(X), so default heights are f(a)=0.5 and f(b)=2.0. The curve y=f(x) should start at the left vertical boundary above the x-axis, rise gently through the middle, and end higher at b. Fill R with pale blue #c9e5ef at about 70% opacity; curve and disk outline in bright blue #2aa3d8; axes and silhouettes near black #222222; red center point #e74747. Panel (b) solid: generate surface by revolving the profile around the x-axis with vertices (x, f(x) cos theta, f(x) sin theta), theta in [0,2pi]. Default solid length is 3.75 world units from X=0.25 to X=4, with radius increasing from 0.5 to 2.0. Draw the top and bottom visible profile curves in black, plus end disks at X=a and X=b as circular caps that project visually as vertical ellipses. The highlighted slice at slider value x is a circular disk in the plane X=x with radius r=f(x); display numeric radius r and area A=pi*r^2. If edited f(x) is negative on part of the interval, use radius |f(x)| for the solid but warn that the standard disk-method figure assumes f(x) >= 0. If a>b, swap or reject with an inline parse/interval error. The x-slider should be dynamically remapped to the current parsed interval [a,b] even though its default range is [0.25,4].
interactionPlan.notes: Render panel (a) as flat 2D line and filled polygon geometry. Render panel (b) as a lathe/revolution mesh with 96 angular segments and at least 160 samples along x for smoothness. Use a semi-transparent solid material so the highlighted disk remains visible; draw silhouette/profile curves as separate thick line overlays. Keep the source-like side view by default, with optional orbit enabled only in the solid view. Recompute the 2D polygon, 3D lathe mesh, end caps, highlighted disk, radius brace, and area/radius readouts whenever the equation fields or x-slider change. Equation parser should support common functions such as sqrt, sin, cos, exp, log, abs, and powers.

authoredContext:
Let f be continuous and nonnegative on [a, b], and let R be the region that is bounded above by y = f (x), below by the x-axis, and on the sides by the lines x = a and x = b (Figure 5.2.9a). Find the volume of the solid of revolution that is generated by revolving the region R about the x-axis. We can solve this problem by slicing. For this purpose, observe that the cross section
of the solid taken perpendicular to the x-axis at the point x is a circular disk of radius f (x)
(Figure 5.2.9b). The area of this region is
A(x) = π[f (x)]

Because the cross sections are disk shaped, the application of this formula is called the
method of disks

Panel (a): the 2D xy-plane showing region R bounded above by the curve y = f(x), below by the x-axis, and between x = a and x = b; a rotation arrow at x = b indicates revolution about the x-axis. Panel (b): a 3D perspective of the resulting solid; at a generic position x along the axis, a circular disk cross-section is highlighted in blue with radius f(x) labeled, showing that each cross-section perpendicular to the x-axis is a disk of area pi[f(x)]^2. The figure derives the disk method formula V = integral from a to b of pi[f(x)]^2 dx by identifying the cross-sectional area at each x and integrating along the axis of revolution.
plan.authoredInteractions:
- equation_input for f(x) and the interval: one field pre-filled with "sqrt(x)" and two fields for bounds a and b; learner edits the function or bounds and the 2D region R redraws, the disk cross-section updates, and the 3D solid of revolution reshapes — teaches that the disk radius at each x equals f(x), so the solid's profile is determined entirely by the formula
- slider for x in [a, b]: sweep the disk cross-section and display radius f(x) and disk area π[f(x)]² at the current position
plan.sourcePath: Anton, Bivens, and Davis. Calculus, 10th Edition, Figure 5.2.9
